In [1]:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import altair as alt

Cleaning Text¶

Given the below example data, clean it up in the following ways:

  1. Replace the British spellings ('yoghurt' and 'flavour') with the American spellings ('yogurt' and 'flavor'), in one line.
  2. Identify the rows that contain the word "mixed".
  3. Use a regular expression to extract the words that come before "mixed". Hint: look at the group constructs in the regex101 quick reference.
  4. Use a split to get the second sentence in a string. Then, fuzzy match to get the correct spelling of Dwight's name.
In [2]:
names = ['Jim','Pam','Dwight']
mystrings = pd.Series(["You are the worst assistant ever and you're disgusting. Dwigt.",
                 "Pam's favorite flavour of yoghurt, which is mixed berry.",
                 "Jim said mixed berries? Oh, well, yeah he's on to me."])
In [3]:
mystrings_clean = mystrings.str.replace(r'flavour|yoghurt', 
                                        lambda m: {'flavour':'flavor','yoghurt':'yogurt'}[m.group(0)],
                                        regex=True)
In [4]:
contains_mixed = mystrings_clean.str.contains(r"\bmixed\b", case=False)
contains_mixed
Out[4]:
0    False
1     True
2     True
dtype: bool
In [5]:
before_mixed = mystrings_clean.str.extract(r"(\b\w+\b)\s+mixed", expand=False)
before_mixed
Out[5]:
0     NaN
1      is
2    said
dtype: object
In [6]:
second_sentence = mystrings_clean.str.split(r"\.\s*", expand=False).str[1]
second_sentence
Out[6]:
0    Dwigt
1         
2         
dtype: object
In [7]:
from difflib import get_close_matches

corrected_name = second_sentence.apply(
    lambda x: get_close_matches(x, names, n=1, cutoff=0.3)[0]
              if isinstance(x, str) and get_close_matches(x, names, n=1, cutoff=0.3)
              else np.nan
)
corrected_name

Text Analysis¶

Step 1: Use the string manipulation you just learned remove the spaces and apostrophes in the column names in the following dataset.¶

In [9]:
# Cleaning column names by removing spaces and apostrophes
pets.columns = (
    pets.columns
        .str.replace(" ", "", regex=False)# remove spaces
        .str.replace("'", "", regex=False)# remove apostrophes
)

Step 2: Explore the Data¶

  • How many unique names are there?
  • Are there similar names that are spelled differently?
  • How many names does each pet have? Is there a pattern you can pull out from that?
  • Do any names stand out to you?
  • Could there be any relationships between names and breeds, species, or zip codes?

Leave all your exploration steps here to show what you looked at.

In [14]:
num_unique_names = pets.AnimalsName.nunique()
num_unique_names
#to see how many unique pet names are there
Out[14]:
15795

With 15,795 unique pet names, Seattle pets showcase a wide variety of names. This indicates high levels of personalization and creativity by owners.

possible_variants = {}
for name in names_lower.unique():
    matches = get_close_matches(name, names_lower.unique(), n=5, cutoff=0.85)
    if len(matches) > 1:
        possible_variants[name] = matches

Cats and dogs share a number of popular names like Lucy, Bella, and Luna. However, dogs tend to have more frequently repeated names, meaning you'll encounter more Lucys and Charlies among them. On the other hand, livestock names often stand out for their uniqueness, with monikers such as “Fuzzy Peaches” and “Heidi.”

This leads to a couple of observations: dogs typically have more conventional or trendy names, while cats showcase a wider variety and fewer instances of repeated names.

Summary

  • Seattle’s pet registry contains 15,795 unique pet names, showing very high naming diversity.
  • Top names include Lucy, Bella, Charlie, Max, and Luna.
  • Most pets have one-word names, but a small number have long or humorous names.
  • Cats and dogs share many of the same popular names, but dogs show more repeated names.
  • Certain breeds (e.g., Retrievers) tend to have classic, common names.
  • ZIP codes show both common names and unique neighborhood-specific naming patterns.
  • Several unusual or themed names appear, showing owner creativity.

Step 3: Come up with a question/goal¶

Pick 3 interesting name patterns that you found in your exploration above.

  • How could you visualize these patterns?
  • What marks and encodings would work well for these visualization?
  • Is there any external data that would be useful?
  • What text manipulation will you have to do before attempting to plot the data?

From the text analysis in Step 2, I selected three compelling naming patterns:

  • Name popularity differs between species: visualize with a grouped bar chart.
    • How does the popularity of the top 10 pet names differ across species (Dogs vs Cats)?
    • Marks and Encodings-Mark: bar; X-axis: pet name; Y-axis: count of licenses; Color: species (Dog vs Cat); Tooltip: exact count per species
    • Bar charts are strong for categorical comparison, and color encoding clearly separates species groups.
    • Text manipulation needed-Normalize names to lowercase, Remove punctuation, Collapse alternate spellings if necessary, Filter to top N most frequent names
  • Multi-word names vary across neighborhoods: visualize Bar Chart or with a ZIP code map.
    • Which neighborhoods (ZIP codes) have the highest proportion of long or multi-word pet names?
    • External Data Needed: A Seattle ZIP code GeoJSON file
    • Text manipulation required: Compute NameCount by splitting names on spaces, Remove quotes before counting words, Possibly remove middle initials or abbreviations
  • Some breeds consistently use the same human-like names: visualize with a heatmap.
    • Do top dog breeds share the same popular human-like names?
    • A heatmap where rows are breeds and columns are top names, with intensity showing frequency.
    • Marks and Encodings-Mark: rect, X-axis: name, Y-axis: breed, Color: count of licenses (darker = more pets with that name), Tooltip: counts and percentages
    • Text manipulation required - Standardize breed names (remove punctuation, collapse duplicates), convert names to lowercase, Filter to top N most common names and top N dog breeds, Pivot into a name × breed matrix

Step 4: Make visualizations¶

Code up some visualizations for the 3 questions in Step 3. Make sure to revisit your questions, ensure the visualization addresses them effectively, and iterate through the EDA process. Ensure that all your plots here are labeled appropriately.

# Normalize names
pets['name_clean'] = pets.AnimalsName.str.lower().str.strip()

# Get top 10 names overall
top10 = (
    pets['name_clean']
    .value_counts()
    .head(10)
    .index
)

# Filter to top 10
df_top10 = pets[pets['name_clean'].isin(top10)]
In [25]:
chart1 = (
    alt.Chart(df_top10)
    .mark_bar()
    .encode(
        x=alt.X('name_clean:N', title='Pet Name', sort=top10),
        y=alt.Y('count()', title='Number of Licenses'),
        color=alt.Color('Species:N', title='Species'),
        tooltip=['Species', 'count()']
    )
    .properties(
        width=500,
        height=350,
        title='Popularity of Top 10 Pet Names by Species'
    )
)
chart1
Out[25]:

Popularity of Top 10 Pet Names by Species

This stacked bar chart shows the top 10 pet names for dogs, cats, and livestock. Dogs dominate the data, evident from the taller orange bars, although cats remain a significant part of the popular names.

Lucy is the most common name for both cats and dogs, followed by Bella and Charlie. This aligns with national trends, indicating a preference for human-style names among Seattle pet owners. Names like Max, Luna, and Sophie also appear across both species.

Key takeaways from the chart include:

  • Many popular names are shared between cats and dogs.
  • Dogs greatly influence the total counts for each name.
  • Name popularity reflects owner choices more than species differences.

Overall, the chart clearly highlights the similarities and differences in naming patterns across species.

# Which ZIP codes have the highest proportion of long or multi-word pet names?

# Convert ZIPs to string
pets['ZIPCode'] = pets['ZIPCode'].astype(str)

# Keep only valid Seattle ZIPs: exactly 5 digits AND starting with '981'
valid_pets = pets[pets['ZIPCode'].str.match(r'^981\d{2}$')]


# Computing average name length per ZIP
zip_stats_clean = (
    valid_pets.groupby('ZIPCode')['NameCount']
    .mean()
    .reset_index()
    .rename(columns={'NameCount': 'avg_name_words'})
)


chart2= (
    alt.Chart(zip_stats)
    .mark_bar()
    .encode(
        y=alt.Y('ZIPCode:N', title='ZIP Code', sort='-x'),
        x=alt.X('avg_name_words:Q', title='Average Number of Words in Pet Names'),
        tooltip=['ZIPCode', 'avg_name_words']
    )
    .properties(
        width=450,
        height=700,
        title='Neighborhoods with the Longest Pet Names'
    )
)
chart2

After cleaning up invalid ZIP codes and filtering for those that actually exist in Seattle, I created a horizontal bar chart showcasing the Top 20 ZIP codes with the highest average number of words in pet names. This revised visualization is much clearer than the original, which was cluttered with hundreds of ZIP codes and hard-to-read text labels.

Now, this chart effectively highlights the neighborhoods that have the most elaborate or multi-word pet names. ZIP codes like 98175 and 98145 stand out, boasting averages close to 2 words per name, pointing to more creative or human-like naming patterns. Most ZIP codes hover around 1.0 to 1.2 words, reinforcing that single-word names remain the norm.

By switching to a horizontal layout and narrowing the focus to the top 20 ZIP codes, I significantly enhanced both readability and interpretability, which aligns with the best practices for plotting categorical text data.

Top 20 Neighborhoods with the Longest Pet Names

This bar chart displays the Seattle ZIP codes with the highest average number of words in pet names. By filtering for valid ZIP codes and focusing on the top 20, the data is clearer.

ZIP codes 98175, 98145, and 98195 have average name lengths of 1.8–2.0 words, indicating a trend towards longer or more creative pet names in these areas, likely due to cultural influences or a younger population near North Seattle and the University District.

Most other top ZIP codes average around 1.1–1.3 words, suggesting that single-word names like “Max” and “Bella” remain popular. This variation highlights differences in naming styles by neighborhood, reflecting cultural or demographic trends.

Overall, this visualization shows where multi-word pet names are common and highlights geographic differences in naming behavior.

In [51]:
import geopandas as gpd
import json


def fix_geojson(data):
    props = [val['properties'] for val in data['features']]
    df = pd.DataFrame.from_dict(props)

    if 'type' in df.columns:
        df['proptype'] = df['type']
    df['type'] = 'Feature'

    geoms = [val['geometry'] for val in data['features']]
    df['geometry'] = geoms

    # Handle Points (not needed here)
    if geoms[0]['type'] == 'Point':
        df['lon'] = [geom['coordinates'][0] for geom in geoms]
        df['lat'] = [geom['coordinates'][1] for geom in geoms]

    return alt.Data(values=df.to_dict(orient='records'))

        color=alt.Color('count:Q', title='Number of Dogs'),

        height=300,
        title='Name Popularity Across Top Dog Breeds'
    )

chart3
Out[29]:

Name Popularity Across Top Dog Breeds (Heatmap)

This heatmap shows the frequency of popular dog names among the five most common breeds in Seattle. Darker colors indicate higher counts, highlighting naming trends.

Retriever breeds (Golden and Labrador) have high frequencies for names like Lucy, Bella, Charlie, and Max, reflecting their popularity and owners’ preferences.

Interestingly, the Domestic Shorthair cat breed, although not a dog, displays high frequencies for Lucy and Luna, indicating these names are popular across species.

Key takeaways from the heatmap:

  • Names like Lucy, Bella, and Charlie are universally popular across breeds.
  • Names such as Buddy, Lily, and Lola are used moderately and vary by breed.
  • Name choices show clear patterns linked to breed type.

This visualization effectively demonstrates that many dog breeds share popular human-style names, revealing consistent naming trends in the dog-owning community.

Final: Bad Text¶

Take the plot that you find the most interesting and recreate it here. Rather than making the text (title, labels, caption, etc) excellent, make it exceptionally bad (keeping it reasonable/readable). Below your graphic, write a description of why the designs and language is a poor choice.

bad_chart = (
    alt.Chart(df_top10)
    .mark_bar()
    .encode(
        x=alt.X('name_clean:N', title='x', sort=top10),
        y=alt.Y('count()', title='y'),
        color='Species'
    )
    .properties(
        title='THIS IS A CHART ABOUT NAMES AND STUFF THAT I FOUND IN THE DATA OMG LOOK AT IT',
        width=700,
        height=500
    )
)

bad_chart
Out[38]:

This plot intentionally ignores key design principles:

  • The title is too long, vague, and unprofessional. It doesn't clarify what the visualization shows and uses distracting language like “OMG LOOK AT IT,” hurting its credibility.

  • The axis labels are meaningless, labeled simply as “x” and “y.” They provide no information about the variables or units, forcing viewers to guess.

  • The caption is confusing and unhelpful. It adds unnecessary noise, expressing uncertainty with phrases like “maybe not sure” and fails to offer useful insights about the data.

  • The title has inconsistent capitalization, which makes it seem chaotic and sloppy.

  • The color legend is poorly labeled, leaving users without clear guidance on what the colors represent.

Overall, the style does not follow data visualization best practices, as the text distracts and confuses rather than aids in interpretation. This example highlights how poor text choices can undermine the clarity and professionalism of a visualization.
